newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Solana says NATO expansion will not end in Madrid.
newsitem.headline: Solana says NATO expansion will not end in Madrid.

text.p: NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana said on Friday that next week's NATO summit in Madrid, where some former communist enemies will be invited to join the alliance, would mark the start and not the end of enlargement.

"Madrid is the moment when a new NATO is defined for a new Europe," Solana told reporters. "Madrid is not the end, Madrid is just the beginning," he added in comments clearly designed to soothe the ruffled feathers of those left out.
Solana, who has failed to find a consensus on how many applicants to invite into the alliance in a first wave, said he was confident the summit would be a success.

Former Warsaw pact foes Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are virtually certain to be invited to join the West's military shield, but France and Italy, backed by other European allies, wanted Romania and Slovenia included as well.

President Bill Clinton has ruled out a broader expansion, saying only the leading three countries are currently ready for membership, but pledging to leave open the door to other central and eastern European states to join at a later date.

"It is not just a question of ticking boxes, enlargement has also to be beneficial to European security as a whole," one senior NATO official said. "At the moment, some members do not feel certain countries do that."
NATO sources say a final decision on who to invite to join the alliance will have to be debated next Tuesday, the first day of the two-day summit, by the 16 heads of government themselves.

NATO says only countries with a mixed economy and a functioning democracy, including democratic control of the armed forces, and with no disputes with neighbouring states can even be considered for membership.
But beyond that, diplomats say enlargement is essentially a political decision.
"At the end of the day, everyone must feel right. You can make a country accept someone they are not happy about," added another diplomat.

All NATO states have said the door will remain open, but have yet to agree the language of the communique to be issued in Madrid, with some countries wanting firm commitments, including dates and possibly names for future waves.
"The 'open door' language is clearly linked to the question of who gets in, and will only be settled at the same time," added the official.

Clinton has said Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are currently the only countries "that can start tomorrow and within a reasonable time meet the same standards of membership militarily that the other NATO countries met".
"I don't forsee any circumstances under which I would change my position that today we ought to have three," Clinton added.

Supporters of enlargement say even a limited expansion will erase forever the artificial division of Europe created by the Cold War and inaugurate a new era of European security with NATO at its centre.

NATO cleared the way for enlargement with a landmark security deal with Russia last May under which it undertook to give Moscow a permanent voice -- enshrined in a new NATO-Russia Council -- in the new European security architecture.
The Madrid summit is also set to endorse formally a similar accord with the Ukrairne.

"This will truly be an historic summit. Even five years ago, who would have thought these countries would be joining a NATO which itself is cooperating with Russia in a host of areas?" added another diplomat.
France however has said it will not be using the summit to announce a return to the alliance's military wing, which it quit in 1966 in a row over U.S. dominance.
Paris maintains not enough progress has yet been made towards creating a separate European identity within the alliance, but has pledged to carry on working to this aim.
